title: BAFTA Trustees Accused of Potentially Violating Charity Law Over Free Ceremony Tickets
description: BAFTA trustees may have violated U.K. charity and company laws by accepting complimentary awards show tickets that were not disclosed in the organi
body:
BAFTA trustees may have violated U.K. charity and company laws by accepting complimentary awards show tickets that were not disclosed in the organization’s financial accounts, according to allegations raised at the British Academy’s annual general meeting this week.

	Michael Pritchett, chair of BAFTA’s membership council, said legal advice he commissioned suggested that trustees who approved the organization’s accounts may have committed offenses under the Charities Act and Companies Act, The Guardian reported Wednesday.
	

	The British Academy of Film and Television Arts, which operates as a registered charity, previously allowed trustees to bring guests to its ceremonies, a practice that is said to have been in place for as long as two decades. The complimentary seats reportedly included premium tickets to the BAFTA Film Awards valued at up to £2,000 ($2,660).

	Pritchett raised the concerns at BAFTA’s annual general meeting on Monday, arguing that the ticket arrangements conflicted with the organization’s governing rules, which prohibit trustees from receiving remuneration or other benefits from the charity.

	The allegations also raise questions about BAFTA’s financial disclosures. The organization’s 2024 and 2025 accounts stated that trustees received no remuneration for their services, while its public register reported no payments or benefits.

	According to Pritchett, the legal advice suggested that trustees who approved those accounts may have violated their obligations under U.K. law. He also questioned whether the complimentary tickets should have been subject to taxes dating back to 2016, potentially leaving BAFTA liable for unpaid National Insurance contributions.
	

	Pritchett called for trustees to repay any money owed, settle outstanding taxes and correct the organization’s financial accounts if necessary. He also criticized a senior BAFTA executive for declining to provide records identifying which trustees had received a complimentary ticket. 

	BAFTA discontinued its longstanding guest-ticket policy in 2025 following a recommendation from its governance committee. The organization has since launched an independent review into the long-running arrangement. 

	BAFTA’s outgoing chair, Sara Putt, said the organization had already taken the steps to address the concerns and noted that Pritchett’s legal advice was based on limited information, while BAFTA’s own legal advisers had access to a more complete account of the circumstances. 

	“Trustees of BAFTA are invited to attend events in a working capacity, representing the Academy in an ambassadorial role, and prior to 2025 they could also bring a ‘plus one’ guest to accompany them,” a BAFTA spokesperson told Variety. “In 2025 BAFTA decided to review its guest tickets arrangements and discontinued the long-standing custom and practice of trustees inviting a plus one. The Board has since established an independent review group to consider the historic guest ticket arrangement – the review is underway.”

	No legal violations have been formally established.

title: ‘Everyone in My Family Has Killed Someone’ Series Adds Eight, Including Sean Astin, Patricia Clarkson
description:
Amazon’s upcoming series adaptation of “Everyone in My Family Has Killed Someone” has added eight new series regulars, Variety has learned. 

	Patr
body:
Amazon’s upcoming series adaptation of “Everyone in My Family Has Killed Someone” has added eight new series regulars, Variety has learned. 

	Patricia Clarkson (“Sharp Objects,” “Pieces of April”), Elizabeth Marvel (“Disclosure Day,” “Presumed Innocent”), Daniella Garcia (“Diamond,” “Grey’s Anatomy”), Felix Solis (“Ozark,” “Sirens”), Sean Astin (“Stranger Things,” “The Lord of the Rings”), Annaleigh Ashford (“Happy Face,” “Welcome to Chippendales”), Chris Walley (“The Young Offenders,” “1917”), and Eliza Bennett (“Sweet/Vicious,” “Dynasty”) have all been cast in the show, which is based on the Benjamin Stevenson novel of the same name. In addition, Alexandra Brodski has boarded the series as executive producer and will direct half the episodes, including both the premiere and the season finale.
	

	The new additions join previously announced series lead Penn Badgley. Described as darkly comedic, the logline for the show states:

	“Set deep in the dense mountains of Vermont’s Northeast Kingdom, the series follows Ern Cunningham (Badgley), a mystery-writing expert who reluctantly attends a family reunion to welcome his brother Michael home from prison — the same brother Ern helped convict. When a frozen body appears and a snowstorm traps everyone inside, the deaths begin to mount. Everyone in his family has already killed someone – either by accident or otherwise.”

	David Hemingson is attached to adapt the murder mystery book and serve as showrunner and executive producer. Bruna Papandrea, Steve Hutensky, and Jeanne Snow of Made Up Stories will also executive produce, as will Molly Allen and Brodski. Badgley will executive produce in addition to starring, with Stevenson also executive producing. Amazon MGM Studios, Fifth Season, and Made Up Stories will co-produce.
	

	Clarkson is repped by CAA and Entertainment 360. Marvel is repped by Verve, Viking Entertainment, and Franklin, Weinrib, Rudell + Vassallo LLP. Garcia is repped by Linden Entertainment and Realm Talent. Solis is repped by D2 Management. Astin is repped by Stewart Talent, Luber / Roklin and Brecheen, Feldman, Breimer, Silver, Thompson. Ashford is repped by CAA and Beth Rosner Management. Walley is repped by Curtis Brown and Canopy Media Partners. Bennett is repped by Affirmative Entertainment and The Artist’s Partnership.

title: ‘PUBG’ Live-Action Series From Donald Glover, Stephen Glover in Development at Netflix
description: Netflix is developing a live-action series based on the battle royale video game “PlayerUnknown’s Battlegrounds” (“PUBG“) with Donald Glover attach
body:
Netflix is developing a live-action series based on the battle royale video game “PlayerUnknown’s Battlegrounds” (“PUBG“) with Donald Glover attached to star. 

	In addition to starring, Glover and his brother and frequent collaborator Stephen Glover will write and executive produce the “PUBG” show, with Donald also planning to direct. Michael Schaefer of Neon TV will also executive produce, as will Fam Udeorji for Gilga, and Taeseok Jang and Sujin Lee for LV3H, the entertainment division of “PUBG” publisher Krafton. 
	

	“PUBG” was originally published by Krafton in 2017. The game does not have a plot, but rather sees large numbers of players dropped into one of several maps featuring a wide array of weapons, vehicles, and other items in a last-man standing deathmatch. Exact plot details for the potential show are under wraps.

	“PUBG” is one of the most popular video games in the world even nearly 10 years after it was released. It broke multiple Guiness world records upon its initial release and continues to pull in hundreds of thousands of active users daily.  

	Donald and Stephen most famously worked together on the hit FX series “Atlanta.” Donald created and starred in the show, with Stephen serving as a writer and executive producer throughout its four-season run. They then teamed on the Amazon series “Swarm” and the musical film “Guava Island,” with Stephen also writing for Donald’s Amazon series “Mr. and Mrs. Smith.” 

	Donald is also known for his work on shows like “Community” and “30 Rock,” as well as for starring in films like “The Martian,” “Spider-Man Homecoming,” “Solo: A Star Wars Story,” and “The Super Mario Galaxy Movie.” 
	

	Donald is repped by The Team and Johnson Shapiro Slewett & Kole. Stephen is repped by WME and Ginsburg Daniels Kallis. 

	Should the “PUBG” show go forward, it would be the latest video game adaptation to find a home at Netflix. The streamer is currently at work on an “Assassin’s Creed” TV series and a “Gears of War” live-action film. Animated series based on games like “Clash of Clans” and “Minecraft” are also in the works, while Netflix currently airs shows like “Splinter Cell: Deathwatch” and “Cyberpunk: Edgerunners.”

schema.headline: ‘PUBG’ Live-Action Series From Donald Glover, Stephen Glover in Development at Netflix

title: ‘The Other Bennet Sister’: Mary Settles Into Married Life in New Images From Upcoming Christmas Special (EXCLUSIVE)
description: “The Other Bennet Sister” has revealed more first-look images at its upcoming Christmas special, giving a sneak peek into how Mary (Ella Bruccoleri
body:
“The Other Bennet Sister” has revealed more first-look images at its upcoming Christmas special, giving a sneak peek into how Mary (Ella Bruccoleri) settles into married life with Tom Hayward (Dónal Finn). 

	Production recently wrapped in Wales on the three-part special, which is produced by Bad Wolf for the BBC and BritBox. It sees the return of Ruth Jones as Mrs. Bennet, Tanya Reynolds as Caroline Bingley, Laurie Davidson as Mr. Ryder, Poppy Gilbert as Lizzie Darcy, Maddie Close as Jane Bingley, Grace Hogg-Robinson as Lydia Wickham and Molly Wright as Kitty Buncock. Nerys Amber Stocks is also joining the cast for the special as Lucy, the Haywards’ housekeeper.
	

	The “Pride & Prejudice” spinoff follows the adventures of Mary, the often overlooked sister in Jane Austen’s beloved 1813 novel. The Christmas special picks up after Mary and Tom have wed. “With marriage comes a new identity, and the question remains: who will Mary become as Mrs. Hayward?” reads its official synopsis. “But just as Mary begins this new chapter, an unexpected visitor from her past arrives at her door in need of her help…”

	Screenwriter Sarah Quintrell, who penned nine of the original season’s 10 episodes, has written all three episodes of the special. Asim Abbasi also returns to direct. 

	After its premiere in March, “The Other Bennet Sister” became the biggest new drama across all platforms in streamers in the U.K. since the previous March, with 6.5 million watching in its first 28 days. Episode 1 is now up to 9.5 million viewers. It also broke records on BritBox, driving five times more new subscribers than any previous launch and achieving the highest streaming rate of any title launch on the service. 
	

	A release date has not yet been set for the special, but it will air in the U.S. and Canada on BritBox and in the U.K. on BBC iPlayer and BBC One. See more first-look images below.

title: ‘Queen Sugar’ Author to Develop Novel ‘Friends and Family’ Into Series With UTV, Mary J. Blige, Gina Prince-Bythewood
description:
Universal Television is developing a series take on the Natalie Baszile novel “Friends and Family,” Variety has learned. 

	The TV version is curre
body:
Universal Television is developing a series take on the Natalie Baszile novel “Friends and Family,” Variety has learned. 

	The TV version is currently titled “Good People.” Should the project go forward, it would be the second series based on one of Baszile’s books. Her novel “Queen Sugar” was previously adapted into the series of the same name, which aired for seven seasons on OWN. 


	The logline for “Good People” states, “Set in Northern California, the story follows Babs, a successful self-made interior designer, and her old money best friend, Nora. Their world cracks open when a series of events, including an affair and a police confrontation involving Nora’s adopted Black son, disrupts the stability of both families and their carefully constructed lives.” 
	

	Marissa Jo Cerar (“13 Reasons Why,” “Black Cake”) is attached to write and executive produce the adaptation. Gina Prince-Bythewood (“Love & Basketball,” “A Different World”) and Reggie Rock Bythewood (“A Different World,” “Swagger”) will both executive produce via Undisputed Cinema, with Prince-Bythewood also onboard to direct the pilot. Debra Martin Chase of Martin Chase Productions will also executive produce, as will Mary J. Blige via Blue Butterfly Productions. Baszile is also attached to executive produce. Universal Television is the studio. 

	The Bythewoods recently returned to “A Different World” with the sequel series that debuted on Netflix in September and has already been renewed for Season 2. Prince-Bythewood is also the co-writer and director of the upcoming film adaptation of the novel “Children of Blood and Bone.” 
	

	Martin Chase’s movie credits include the Oscar-nominated “Harriet” as well as franchises like “The Princess Diaries,” “The Sisterhood of the Traveling Pants,” and “The Cheetah Girls.” 

	Cerar is repped by Heroes and Villains Entertainment, CAA, and attorney Kim Stenton. Prince-Bythewood is repped by CAA and Del Shaw Moonves. Rock Bythewood is repped by CAA. Martin Chase is repped by CAA and Del Shaw Moonves. Blige is repped by IAG, Laffitte Management Group and LaPolt Law. Baszile is repped by Heroes and Villains Entertainment and Hirsch Wallerstein.

	(Pictured, left to right: Natalie Baszile, Mary J. Blige, Gina Prince-Bythewood, Debra Martin Chase, Reggie Rock Bythewood, Marissa Jo Cerar)

title: ‘The Bold and the Beautiful’ Star Heather Tom on Potentially Breaking a Daytime Emmys Acting Record This Friday
description: Heather Tom could make history this Friday at the 53rd annual Daytime Emmys. “The Bold and the Beautiful” star is in line to win her seventh Daytim
body:
Heather Tom could make history this Friday at the 53rd annual Daytime Emmys. “The Bold and the Beautiful” star is in line to win her seventh Daytime Emmy, which would give her the most wins by an actress in daytime history. As it now stands, “The Bold and the Beautiful” star is tied with Erika Slezak (“One Life to Live”) at six each. 

	Tom scored a nomination this year in the outstanding lead actress in a daytime drama field (her first nod in the category since 2020, when she won) for playing Katie Logan on “B&B.” But that’s not all: This year, Tom is also nominated as part of the writing staff on “Bold and the Beautiful,” in the outstanding writing team for a daytime drama series category.
	

	“It’s kind of crazy,” she tells Variety of her rare double nomination. “I love the night. [Daytime is] a very small community, and I’ve known most of these people for literally most of my life. It’s always nice to be recognized and to go and hang, and two in one night seems insane!”

	READ MORE: Daytime Emmys Announce 2026 Nominations: ‘The Young and the Restless’ Leads, ‘Beyond the Gates’ Thrives In Its First Year (Full Nominations List)

	Tom won her first Daytime Emmy in 1993 in the outstanding younger actress in a drama series category for “The Young and the Restless,” followed by another one for “Y&R” in the same category in 1999. As part of “The Bold and the Beautiful,” she won the Daytime Emmy for supporting actress in 2011, followed by lead actress wins in 2012, 2013 and 2020. She’s the only performer to ever win Daytime Emmys in all three classifications of younger, supporting and lead.
	

	Slezak won all six of her Daytime Emmys in lead actress (for “One Life to Live” in 1984, 1986, 1992, 1995, 1996 and 2005) and will continue to hold the most acting wins in a single category. But when all acting categories are counted, Tom could surpass Slezak this year for most overall wins. But Tom stresses that she doesn’t feel like she’s in competition with the daytime icon.

	“I don’t think I could be in a rivalry with Erica Slezak because she’s just iconic,” Tom says. “It kind of floors me to think that I’m kind of in the same conversation as her, because I was such a huge fan. I had the honor working with her and I just loved every single second. She always just brought it. There was never a day where she phoned it in. I certainly cannot feel like I’m in the rivalry with her because I would just have to say that she’s already won.”

	Tom notes that her favorite Daytime Emmy tradition was actually started by Slezak and another former winner, Susan Flannery (“Bold and the Beautiful”): an annual actress nominees’ lunch, organized by whoever won the previous year.

	“We have the leading ladies’ lunch, and it’s something that Susan Flannery and Erica Slezak actually created,” Tom says. “My favorite thing to do is get together with all these amazing ladies and just have a good hang. We let our hair down and dish a little bit and run up the bill for whomever’s paying. It’s really my favorite part about being nominated.”

	As for her other nomination in writing, Tom credits “Bold and the Beautiful” executive producer and head writer Brad Bell for giving her the opportunity behind the camera. 

	“He’s always been extremely supportive of what I’ve wanted to do and branching out,” she says. “I’ve been doing daytime now for, gosh, almost 37 years. Along the way I kind of wanted to start trying other things. I write extensively outside of the show and have a bunch of things that I’m pitching right now. Brad allowed me to do a spec script because he knows that I’ve been wanting to write for the show for a while. And then he kind of gave me an opportunity to do a few scripts. He expects a lot from the people who work for him in all capacities. And so I think as long as I deliver, he’ll give me the opportunity and I couldn’t be more grateful for that. It’s really rare to have a boss who’s willing to encourage all aspects of my career.”
	

	That’s why, if she does win on Friday, “the only person that I absolutely 100% have to thank is Brad,” she says. “And as long as I get his name out, then I’ve done my job. And then, second is my husband. That’s kind of all I have in my brain.”

	The 53rd Daytime Emmys, which recognizes daytime dramas, talk series, entertainment news, culinary, adventure, instructional and legal/courtroom programming, takes place Friday in Los Angeles at Hollywood’s Palladium. “The Young and the Restless” leads all programs with 18 nominations this year, followed by newcomer “Beyond the Gates,” with 15. “General Hospital” icon Genie Francis is set to receive the lifetime achievement award. There is no host this year.

	Meanwhile, as “Bold and the Beautiful” marks its 40th season, the show also recently launched an app where its entire episodic catalog lives. Tom believes that the streaming age has helped expose the soap to new audiences.

	“People used to have to tape it on their VCR. Now they don’t have to do that; it’s right at their fingertips,” Tom says. “I think a younger generation is discovering it, and people who used to watch are coming back to it. I also feel like Brad is really kind of taking the show back to its roots and focusing on family and fashion. ‘The Bold and the Beautiful’ has always been a fun show. We’re high melodrama, of course, because we’re a soap opera and everything is life and death. But at the same time, there’s been an element of humor to the show from the very beginning, and I think he’s hearkening back to that and it seems like the people who are watching really like it.”

	Tom says she’s revisited old episodes recently because of a current “Bold and the Beautiful” storyline for her character, Katie, that’s inspired by past plots.

	“I’ve kind of gone back and watched some stuff,” she says. “It’s so crazy to think that I’ve been on this show for 20 years. Time just goes by so fast, and I have a hard time even wrapping my head around that. But it’s fun to think that, like, basically my whole life has been documented in one way or the other.”

	Outside of “Bold and the Beautiful,” Tom is busy at work on developing microdramas in a variety of formats.
	

	“It’s the ground floor of what daytime was 50 years ago,” she says of the new format. “We are creating some, and I love that they’re willing to kind of go crazy with them. It can all be about vampires and billionaires, and everyone’s sleeping with everybody else. I mean, I love daytime. I’ve spent my life in this genre, and I love it because the stakes are always so high. It gives you permission to just lay it all out there. It’s fun as an actress, it’s fun as a writer because there are no rules. You can write whatever you want, and then 100% commit to it so that it works. People love watching it, it’s entertaining and it’s a guilty pleasure and all those things are what entertainment should be.”

	Tom says she’s developing microdramas that are inspired by fairy tales and fables, including projects inspired by “Snow White,” “Sleeping Beauty” and “Jack and the Beanstalk.”

	And then, “Of course we have to have our vampire/werewolf one. We’ve really gotten into the lore,” Tom says. “I was like, ‘Let’s write one that has all this accurate stuff about vampires and werewolves and the history and the lore of it.’ So I know more about vampires than I ever needed to know. Honestly, you look at a show like Bridgerton, which is just a Harlequin romance novel, like it’s wildly romantic. People love it, and so that’s what we’re writing. This is my wheelhouse, so I’m having a good time.”

	As “The Bold and the Beautiful” marks its 70th anniversary, Tom says Bell is taking the show back to its roots. 

	“I always say that the daytime is Shakespeare,” she says. “You have these two warring families. You have people coming back from the dead. You have mistaken identity. You have love triangles. It’s for the masses. That’s really what daytime is, and I think that for Brad, he’s going back to what ‘Bold and the Beautiful’ has always been: You have the two strong families, you have the two fashion houses that are going head to head and you really can see those essences of Los Angeles and California and high fashion and couture. It’s about clothes and hair and makeup and sets. It’s fun. So I think for the 40th, that’s where we’re going.”

	The 53rd Daytime Emmys, produced by the National Academy of Television Arts & Sciences, takes place Friday, Oct. 30 at 5 p.m. PT. Watch on YouTube here.

title: Cannes Chief Thierry Fremaux Hails French Film Model as CNC Head Gaëtan Bruel Vows to Fight for Its Future at 80th Anniversary
description: France’s National Film Board, the CNC, marked its 80th anniversary with a three-day gathering of industry leaders in Paris, including Cannes Film F
body:
France’s National Film Board, the CNC, marked its 80th anniversary with a three-day gathering of industry leaders in Paris, including Cannes Film Festival chief Thierry Frémaux who praised the country’s unique film funding system. CNC president Gaëtan Bruel, meanwhile, warned against attempts to dismantle a model that has helped make France a global cinema powerhouse.

	The anniversary celebrations, held from Oct. 26-28 at the Cinémathèque française, came at a particularly fraught moment for the institution which faces growing political scrutiny and budgetary pressures as France heads toward the 2027 presidential election.
	

	Frémaux, who also heads the Institut Lumière in Lyon, highlighted the CNC’s key role on display across films showcased at Cannes and other major festivals.

	“We don’t say it because the Americans accuse us of constantly favoring certain things, because they themselves cannot imagine that the selection process is conducted in complete independence. But you can see just how much French money, the CNC and French professionals are absolutely everywhere,” Frémaux said during an onstage conversation with film historian Antoine de Baecque at the French Cinémathèque on Wednesday.

	Frémaux also pointed out the CNC’s support for film restoration, noting that countries around the world have begun developing similar initiatives.

	“Every country in the world has its masterpieces. And not all masterpieces have been restored, so there is still plenty of work to be done. Many countries are now giving themselves the means to do this, following the French model,” he said.
	

	Frémaux emphasized that France’s film funding system not only supports contemporary production but also helps preserve cinema’s history and nurture future generations of film lovers.

	“People are finally beginning to understand that money from cinema goes back into cinema. It has taken a long time, but I’m starting to read things about it. Journalists are always a little slow,” he joked. “But the fact remains that this money from cinema also goes toward cinema’s history. And that brings us back to the fundamental role of building an educational and intellectual foundation for cinephilia as a driving force in protecting contemporary creation.”

	The event wrapped with a forceful defense of the institution from Bruel, who took over as CNC president last year and is facing pressures from populist parties, including the far right party Rassemblement National. In its latest budget proposal, unveiled earlier this month, the party outlined plans to strip down the National Film Board, privatize public broadcasting and slash public broadcasting funding

	“We are going through, on a global scale, one of the deepest crises this sector has experienced since the invention of cinema,” Bruel said. “These 80 years have not been a smooth ride. They have been marked by successive upheavals. But what we are experiencing today is as though we were facing the ocean head-on, as though the upheavals of eight decades were happening all at once.”

	Bruel also pointed to the industry’s shifting power dynamics, as streaming platforms are now facing new competition from YouTube.

	“A few years ago, streamers seemed to be triumphing over television and movie theaters. Today, faced with YouTube, they themselves are discovering their vulnerabilities, and they are seeking to converge with traditional broadcasters, a sign that yesterday’s world has not said its last word,” he said.

	For Bruel, these changes make the CNC’s mission more important than ever, particularly as public support for the arts faces increasing criticism.

	“According to some, the CNC is a dispensable appendage, and all we would need to do is cut it off to get better. You can always cut off an arm, but you’d better be sure of what you stand to gain and what you stand to lose,” he said.
	

	Bruel argued that France’s film funding model also serves a civic role, in giving people access to culture, through an extensive network of movie theaters, as well as film education programs allowing an estimated two million schoolchildren to visit movie theater each year.

	The CNC’s 80th anniversary brought together a broad cross-section of France’s film and television industries for three days of discussions exploring the institution’s history and its evolving role in the entertainment landscape.

	Among the prominent filmmakers participating were Olivier Assayas, Arnaud Desplechin, Amélie Bonnin and Rachid Hami, alongside producers Anne-Dominique Toussaint, Alex Berger and Simone Harari Baulieu, and leading animation executives including Illumination Studios Paris co-founder Jacques Bled and Xilam Animation founder Marc du Pontavice.

	The program explored the defense of theatrical exhibition, the rise of French animation, the expansion of the CNC’s remit into television, video games and immersive creation, and the challenges posed by Hollywood’s global dominance. A panel devoted to protecting movie theaters featured Desplechin alongside exhibitors Aurélie Delage and Camille Labé, and former UGC chief Alain Sussfeld. Another discussion examined the CNC’s expansion into television, bringing together Berger, Harari Baulieu, former CNC director general and Arte president Jérôme Clément, and screenwriter-director Clémence Madeleine-Perdrillat.

	Looking ahead, Bruel signaled that the CNC would soon present a broader strategy for digital creators and social media platforms like YouTube, arguing that they should contribute more fairly to the financing of French audiovisual creation, on par with streaming services. 

	His words on investment alluded to the European Commission’s current review of the Audiovisual Media Service Directive which allows members states to require streaming platforms such as Netflix, Disney+ and Prime Video to invest in European film and television production. The review could also open the door to bringing YouTube under similar investment obligations to level the playing field between broadcasters, streamers and digital platforms. 

	“Will we remain one in the future? No battle is lost in advance, especially when we have so many strengths in our hands, and you can count on the CNC to play its full part. But the answer, by definition, remains open,” Bruel concluded.

title: Andrew Tate Docuseries ‘Toxic Empire’ Set at Investigation Discovery
description:
Investigation Discovery (ID) will release a new four-part docuseries on the infamous brothers Andrew and Tristan Tate, Variety has learned. 

	Titl
body:
Investigation Discovery (ID) will release a new four-part docuseries on the infamous brothers Andrew and Tristan Tate, Variety has learned. 

	Titled “Andrew Tate: Toxic Empire,” the four-part series will have its two-hour premiere on Nov. 25 on ID at 9pm ET/PT. Subsequent episodes will roll out on Wednesdays thereafter. It will also be available to stream on HBO Max. 

	ID has also released a trailer for the series, which can be seen below. 
	

	The official description of the series states: 

	“As Andrew Tate built a global following of millions with content promoting wealth, health, male dominance and misogyny, his rise drew both devoted fans and mounting allegations. The docuseries offers a comprehensive look at the story that has dominated headlines, featuring unprecedented access to male followers, insiders, alleged survivors, investigative journalists and extensive Tate archive, to explore how the lines between aspiration and exploitation became blurred.” 

	The docuseries will explore how the brothers recruited male followers and launched their webcam business and what they referred to as their “PhD” (Pimping Hoes Degree) course, which allegedly taught men coercive methods to recruit women into webcamming while retaining most of the profit for themselves. It will also feature interviews with former followers and associates. 

	The series is directed and produced by Julian P. Hobbs, Elli Hakami and Adrian Murray for Investigation Discovery.

	The Tate brothers are currently incarcerated in Miami, FL, while they fight extradition to the United Kingdom, where they are being accused of multiple crimes like rape, human trafficking, and more. The brothers have also been charged in a similar case in Romania.

title: ‘Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom’ Director on Why AI Is Not a Threat: ‘There’s a Desire to See the Craft Behind the Finished Product’
description: “Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom” is launching into Italy as the opener of Lucca Comics and Games on the eve of Halloween, which, coinci
body:
“Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom” is launching into Italy as the opener of Lucca Comics and Games on the eve of Halloween, which, coincidentally, also happens to be when this third feature in the Aardman Animations’ hit stop-motion spinoff franchise is set.

	Matthew Walker, who is the film’s co-director, is clearly pleased to be attending the 60th edition of this unique geek meet held within the 16th century walls of the medieval Tuscan town of Lucca because, as he puts is, “yeah, I am a geek myself.” 
	

	Unsurprisingly, when he meets the Italian press in Lucca, the first question is about whether this new “Shaun the Sheep” entry, famously handmade frame by frame with clay puppets, can be seen as a symbolic bastion against the encroaching spread of AI through filmmaking and the myriad concerns this is raising.

	Walker subsequently sat with Variety and drilled down on why he thinks AI-made animation is not an existential threat for Aardman. At least not for the moment. And why animation films may be more immune to the impact of AI than live action ones. 
	
		You’ve said you don’t think AI can ever really replicate the human aspect of the art of animation. Stop-motion is very much about physical puppets and physical sets, about communicating emotional beats with puppets. Can you tell me more about this part of the creative process?	

	Something I love about stop-motion is the tactile physicality of it and I think that’s what appeals to audiences. You obviously want to tell a funny emotional story with these characters. But on top of that, I think that just the technique of it, the stop motion technique, has a lot of appeal in the knowledge that these are real models all built with incredible detail by the artists. When Aardman release behind-the-scenes footage videos, they are always really popular because people love seeing how stop-motion is made. People really respond to seeing these huge detailed sets with these little puppets, which is obviously something AI can’t replicate. I also think there is a desire for imperfection. We’ve gotten to a point now with digital technology where we can kind of do anything; things can be so beautifully polished. So there’s a desire to kind of step back and bring back some imperfection. You see it in things like [Sony Pictures Animation] “Spider-Verse” franchise, where they’re introducing the 2D element and even hand-drawn pencil lines and stuff. It’s because there’s a desire to see the craft behind the finished product. Like being able to see the pencil lines. In stop motion, it’s about being able to see the fingerprints.
	
	
		In the vaster animation space, there are several animation features from various parts of the world that will be hitting the screens soon. Do you think audiences will be able to tell when something is AI, and therefore possibly disengage emotionally?	

	Yes. At the moment it certainly feels like that’s the case. I know AI is advancing all the time, and we might get to a point where it’s really difficult to tell the difference. But I think at the moment, even when they might not be able to identify what’s not right, I think the audience can kind of tell when something is made with AI because there’s something a little bit uncanny. Something that doesn’t quite feel right. When something is artificial you can tell, even though you can’t necessarily articulate why. AI can replicate art, but I don’t think it can replicate the emotion and reason behind the art. It doesn’t necessarily understand why those pencil lines were made. Whereas I think a human audience recognizes the craftsmanship that goes into something. 
	
		The audience for Aardman IPs such as “Wallace & Gromit,” “Chicken Run” and “Shaun the Sheep,” which all rely on dialogue-free physical comedy, starts with toddlers. Do you think the inherently humanistic nature of these stories can serve as an antidote to AI-made animation?	

	Yes, I think so. With stop motion and the work that Aardman does it’s very much about the characters and the performances of those characters. It’s similar to when you watch a live-action film. You know, with a good actor, you really respond to the emotional performance. And it’s the same with an animated character. The animator puts their own emotions into it. They’re essentially actors themselves, just doing it much more slowly than in live action. I think when you’re watching things from an early age, that becomes part of your knowledge of art and how you respond to it. And you take with you as you grow up.
	
		Regarding live action, which genre do you consider more immune to the threat of AI: live action or animation? 	

	I think animation is. A good animator can turn any object into a character. It’s like the Pixar lamp. it’s just a lamp. It has no face. It has no features. Has no limbs. But the way it’s animated, the way the animators have made it move, allows the audience to have an emotional connection with it. To see it as a character, as a sentient being. And that’s not replicating anything. With live action, by using AI it’s easier to replicate human activity because there’s a vast wealth of footage that AI is fed with. But in animation there isn’t that wealth of footage to work with, because the animation process starts entirely from scratch. If you take a ball or a lamp and give it life, that’s not based on anything. It’s just based on an understanding of what a human can connect with.
	

	This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.



	

									GKIDS

title: Sophie Cunningham Shades Anthem Skippers, Says She's Proud To Be American
description:
Sophie Cunningham
                          Shades National Anthem Skippers
body:
Sophie Cunningham
                          Shades National Anthem Skippers
                          ... 'I'm Proud To Be An American'
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              October 29, 2026
                            10:15 AM PDT
                                                                            
              
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Sophie Cunningham isn't sitting out the debate over WNBA teams skipping the national anthem ... telling Theo Von she's proudly standing with the troops!
      
    
            The hooper and comedian chatted on Theo's "This Past Weekend" podcast this week ... in the wake of the Atlanta Dream and Golden State Valkyries bookin' it from the hardwood before "The Star-Spangled Banner" each and every game of the WNBA Finals.
      
    
            Von asked Cunningham for his thoughts, and Sophie responded ... "You know who you're talking to?"
      

                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The Fever guard didn't call out either team by name -- instead pointing out players have been doing it all season.
      
    
            So, where does she stand? Right next to the military.
      
    
            Sophie revealed she's got family members who've served, and anytime she can shout out veterans and the people currently fighting for the country, she's gonna show them love.
      
    
            Cunningham understands not everyone sees it her way ... but made her own position crystal clear.
      
    
            "I take a lot of pride in where I come from and I'm proud to be an American citizen."
      
    
        Waiting for your permission to load the Twitter Tweet.
      
    
            The controversy has reached the highest levels of the U.S. government. Vice President JD Vance ripped the move, saying players shouldn't protest a politician's policies by disrespecting the country.
      
    
            There's more.
      
    
            She also revealed something scary, saying she's received threats and has been stalked, and it's so serious that the FBI is keeping tabs on roughly 20 people.
      
    
            Cunningham didn't name names, but seemingly isn't lying.
      
    
            A 49-year-old man was arrested in June and is facing felony stalking and intimidation charges, plus misdemeanor harassment.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Heading into the offseason, Sophie could have a new home next year ... she's a free agent.
      
    
            Wherever she winds up, you can bet she'll be on the court for the anthem!
